results.title: Distributed event-triggered communication for dynamic average consensus in networked systems - ScienceDirect
results.content: # Brief paper Distributed event-triggered communication for dynamic average consensus in networked systems☆. This paper presents distributed algorithmic solutions that employ opportunistic inter-agent communication to achieve dynamic average consensus. Our starting point is a continuous-time distributed coordination strategy that, under continuous-time communication, achieves practical asymptotic tracking of the dynamic average of the time-varying agents’ reference inputs. Then, for this algorithm, depending on the directed or undirected nature of the time-varying interactions and under suitable connectivity conditions, we propose two different distributed event-triggered communication laws that prescribe agent communications at discrete time instants in an opportunistic fashion. The dynamic average consensus problem seeks a distributed algorithm that allows a group of agents to track the average of individual time-varying reference inputs, one per agent. *Literature review*: The literature of cooperative control has proposed dynamic average consensus algorithms that are executed either in continuous time (Bai et al., 2010, Freeman et al., 2006, Kia et al., in press, Olfati-Saber and Shamma, 2005, Spanos et al., 2005) or in fixed stepsize discrete time (Kia et al., in press, Zhu and Martínez, 2010). *Statement of contributions*: We propose novel distributed dynamic average consensus algorithms which employ opportunistic strategies to determine the communication times among neighboring agents. By establishing positive lower bounds on the inter-event times of each agent for both cases, we also show that the proposed distributed event-triggered communication laws are free from Zeno behavior (the undesirable situation where an infinite number of communication rounds are triggered in a finite amount of time). We have studied the multi-agent dynamic average consensus problem over networks where inter-agent communication takes place at discrete time instants in an opportunistic fashion. ### Distributed event-triggered control of multi-agent systems with combinational measurements. ### Distributed event-triggered control for multi-agent systems. * ### Event-triggered communication and control of networked systems for multi-agent consensus. (2015b) present event-triggered versions of these algorithms that determine when communication should occur according to some time- or state-varying thresholds over multi-agent networks with single integrator and dynamic topologies. This article provides an introduction to event-triggered coordination for multi-agent average consensus. * ### Robust cooperative output regulation of multi-agent systems via adaptive event-triggered control.

results.title: Constant-Overhead Zero-Knowledge for RAM Programs
results.content: ### Constant-Overhead Zero-Knowledge for RAM Programs. We show a constant-overhead interactive zero-knowledge (ZK) proof system for RAM programs, that is, a ZK proof in which the communication complexity as well as the running times of the prover and verifier scale linearly in the size of the memory $N$ and the running time $T$ of the underlying RAM program. In particular, our implementation supports ZK proofs of private read/write accesses to 64 MB of memory ($2^{24}$ 32-bit words) using only 34 bytes of communication per access, a more than $80\times$ improvement compared to the recent BubbleRAM protocol. We also design a lightweight RISC CPU that can efficiently emulate the MIPS-I instruction set, and for which our ZK proof communicates only $\approx$ 320 bytes per cycle, more than $10\times$ less than the BubbleRAM CPU. In a 100 Mbps network, we can perform zero-knowledge executions of our CPU (with 64 MB of main memory and 4 MB of program memory) at a clock rate of 6.6 kHz.

results.title: How much overhead does the oneagent take? - Dynatrace
results.content: ‎11 Sep 2017 04:32 PM I'll paste the responses with information from dev directly form a support case where this was asked: > **The overhead of the Agent (regarding response time, CPU, memory & network traffic) depends on so many factors and their correlations that it's just impossible to estimate it upfront. > Such factors include, but are not limited to e.g.:** > * **used technologies (Java, .NET, PHP, Apache, node.js, ...)** > * **requests per second (or some other load indicator)** > * **number of concurrently executed threads** > * **amount of remote communication and IO interaction** > * **error handling, e.g. number of thrown exceptions** > * **complexity of the code in general** > * **any potential virtualization in place** > * **inter-process mutexes and other dependencies** > * **from the Agent & configuration perspective:** > * **type of Agent (OS Agent, Java Agent, Network Agent, Log Agent, ...)** > * **number of placed sensors & instrumented methods** > * **level of detail of captured information** > **Measuring the overhead is also non-trivial, as the Agent itself is part of the whole system and can as such not easily measure itself. > To ensure this we execute automated performance tests on a daily basis which will instantly show us if something got better or worse.** _**so here's what we do in terms of overhead measurement and reduction:**_ * _**in Dynatrace & AppMon Special Agents (OneAgent and Classic Agent)**_ * _**check overhead of Auto-Sensors in the process and adapt it to not exceed fixed 1-3% (in Dynatrace, depending on Agent type) or configurable 1%-20% (in AppMon)**_ * _**if network is too slow for the captured data, creation of new PurePaths will be reduced and finally data will be discarded**_ * _**also some Sensors will reduce data capturing when certain limits are reached (e.g. Exception Sensor -> limit stacktrace capturing)**_ * _**in Dynatrace Network Agent**_ * _**turning off the network data collection as soon as CPU reaches certain limit (5% or so)**_ ‎03 Oct 2017 10:47 AM Results may vary, depending on the environment.

Title: RabbitMQ Memory Alarm Triggered - Stack Diagnosis
# RabbitMQ Memory Alarm Triggered. RabbitMQ has reached its memory threshold and stopped accepting new messages. ### Debug rabbitmq automatically with DrDroid AI →. ## What is RabbitMQ Memory Alarm Triggered. RabbitMQ is a robust open-source message broker that facilitates communication between distributed systems by sending and receiving messages. ## Identifying the Symptom: Memory Alarm Triggered. One common issue encountered by RabbitMQ users is the 'Memory Alarm Triggered' warning. This symptom indicates that RabbitMQ has reached its configured memory threshold, causing it to stop accepting new messages until the memory usage is reduced. ## Explaining the Issue: Memory Thresholds in RabbitMQ. RabbitMQ uses memory alarms to prevent excessive memory consumption that could degrade system performance. When the memory usage exceeds a certain percentage of the available memory, RabbitMQ triggers a memory alarm. By default, this threshold is set to 40% of the total available memory. Once triggered, RabbitMQ will block publishers from sending new messages until the memory usage falls below the threshold. ### Why Memory Alarms Occur. Memory alarms typically occur due to high message rates, large message sizes, or insufficient memory allocation for RabbitMQ. It is crucial to monitor and manage memory usage to ensure smooth operation. ## Steps to Fix the Memory Alarm Issue. ### Step 1: Increase Available Memory. Consider increasing the available memory on the server where RabbitMQ is running. ### Step 2: Adjust Memory Thresholds. Modify the memory threshold settings in the RabbitMQ configuration file to better suit your system's capacity. vm\_memory\_high\_watermark.relative = 0.6. This example sets the memory threshold to 60% of the available memory. After making changes, restart RabbitMQ for the new settings to take effect. For more information on optimizing RabbitMQ performance, visit the RabbitMQ Memory Management Guide. Implement monitoring tools to keep track of RabbitMQ's memory usage and performance metrics. Tools like Prometheus and Grafana can help visualize and alert on memory usage trends, allowing you to scale resources proactively. By understanding and addressing the root causes of memory alarms in RabbitMQ, you can ensure that your messaging system remains reliable and efficient. Regular monitoring and configuration adjustments are key to preventing memory-related issues and maintaining optimal performance. Connect your tools and debug with AI.
